speechtext: Again?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: The Minister without Portfolio says, "Again". I will keep saying it again and again, and it is becoming quite apparent these are the facts of life.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: You are entirely wrong.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Then why are you splitting in two in the province of Quebec? You cannot answer that. Liberal forces are splitting in two in the province of Quebec, Canadians in general, and Quebeckers in particular are realizing it is bad for our country and for the province simultaneously to have Liberal governments in Ottawa and Quebec.
Since the present government has come to power in Ottawa Canadians have become appalled at its record in the field of federal-provincial relations. I have no reason to take any pleasure from this fact because this government, I regret, has unnecessarily hurt national unity at a time when all Canadians are preparing to celebrate their centenary. Conservatives believe that because a man is intensely loyal to his family and church there is no reason to hold that his love of country

is diminished. In the province of Quebec our loyalty to provincial ways and customs and to the French fact in no way lessens our true spirit of Canadianism. That Quebeckers love their province does not diminish their love for Canada and the Canadian family. Quebec has always looked upon confederation as a pact under which the provinces have their rights-something which the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues do not seem to realize. If Liberal sectionalism told- and tells-the rest of Canada that this is an extreme type of autonomy which means no co-operation with Ottawa and the other provinces, so much the worse; the story of Cartier, Macdonald and Diefenbaker is a different story.
The Minister without Portfolio, again speaking from his seat, jests. I know all about his smear campaign-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: I am not listening to you. I am reading my paper; that is all.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I know the hon. gentleman reads many papers in this house. No one did more to smear our leader in the province of Quebec. But let me quote from two great men who understood Conservative principles-Salisbury and Burke. In my view these general observations illustrate the universality of Conservative principles even in Canada at the present time. The following is an excerpt from a speech by Lord Salisbury on Conservative policy at Newport on Monday, October 7, 1885. It illustrates the persistence of Conservative advocacy of a more equitable balance of initiative and authority between central and local governments.
He said:
Now bear it mind what true reform in local government means. It does not only mean-what I quite admit-that the local authorities should be popularly elected: but it means that, when you have got at what you want, when you have provided the proper constitution of local authority, you must provide that the local authority has sufficient powers, and that it gets those powers by diminishing the excessive and exaggerated powers which have been heaped on the central authorities in London.
Now let me quote, pertinently I believe, from a speech by Edmund Burke, because it illustrates the traditional Conservative attitude toward the morbid concentration of power in the modern state:
It is boasted that the geometrical policy has been adopted, that all local ideas should be sunk, and that the people should be no longer Gascons, Picards, Bretons, Normans; but Frenchmen, with one country, one heart, and one assembly. But instead of being all Frenchmen, the greater likelihood is that the inhabitants of that region will
Federal-Provincial Relations shortly have no country. No man ever was attached by a sense of pride, partiality, or real affection to a description of square measurements. He never will glory in belonging to the chequer number 71, or to any other badge-ticket. We begin our public affections in our families. No cold relation is a zealous citizen. We pass on to our neighbourhoods, and our habitual provincial connections. These are inns and resting-places. Such divisions of our country as have been formed by habit, and not by a sudden jerk of authority, were so many images of the great country in which the heart found something which it could fill. The love of the whole is not extinguished by this subordinate partiality. Perhaps it is a sort of elemental training to those higher and more large regards by which alone men come to be affected, as with their own concern, in the prosperity of a kingdom. To be attached to the subdivision, to love the little platoon we belong to in society, is the first principle (the germ, as it were) of public affections. It is the first link in the series by which we proceed towards a love of our country, and of mankind.
Sir, I feel these citations are very pertinent to my general opening remarks. Let me close this portion of my observations by saying that Conservative principle with its emphasis on local self agency and its attitude towards the provinces has a most valuable and distinctive contribution to make to the contemporary Canadian scene.
At this point, under the second heading of my remarks, I should like to emphasize a few basic problems in the field of federal-provincial relations. It is my opinion that a great disservice is done when the ordinary fiscal problems connected with federal-provincial relations are confused with the general question of bilingualism and biculturalism. I fully realize that many of the legitimate aspirations of my province are obviously linked with economic considerations. But currently too many people both inside and outside Quebec are confusing the normal demands for the tax dollar with the question of English-French relations. The results are harmful.
I believe there are two main factors militating against a solution to the question of satisfactory federal-provincial fiscal arrangements at the present time. The first, as I said, in my general remarks, is the tendency of the present Liberal administration toward increasing centralization at a time when decentralization is a "must". The second is the lack of consultation with the provinces and the woeful inadequacy of permanent consultative machinery in relation to the provinces. As to the first factor, we should not really be surprised by the current push toward overcentralization in Ottawa today. We in Canada are blessed with a fine civil service

Federal-Provincial Relations but the Prime Minister, a former senior civil servant himself, surrounded by the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Industry, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Justice and others, all former senior bureaucrats is, consciously or subconsciously, taking a centralist position which in my view is simply out of step with the times today.
I repeat, we must have a strong central government, but it must act within its constitutional responsibilities. The present government, however, is neither active nor strong. The Prime Minister rightfully gained a reputation as a wise negotiator. But now he is Prime Minister and he must lead. If he continues to negotiate, and if as well he continues to retain this slavish attachment to outmoded centralist doctrine, the resulting damage to national unity will be incalculable. No real agreement with the provinces on tax and financial matters will ever be attained in these circumstances.
The second factor aggravating the present situation relates to the woeful inadequacy of the permanent consultative machinery dealing with problems arising between Ottawa and the provinces, and the refusal of the present government to consult with the provinces on a genuine basis in the true spirit of co-operative federalism. This government has consulted only under pressure, often too late and, unfortunately for the country only when the damage has been done. The result has been an inability to implement the major part of its domestic program.
For example, the Prime Minister says he has already created a secretariat for federal-provincial relations. But when I made specific inquiries I found the only people in the office are a part time employee-the director-and an assistant. The part time director is also an assistant secretary to the cabinet. So this in fact is merely a sham. After this procedure was set up the Minister of Justice had the effrontery to go into Montreal and before the Canadian club say that this government had set up a federal-provincial secretariat in the Prime Minister's office. This is not the kind of secretariat I am thinking of; I am thinking of a federal-provincial secretariat based on the ARDA approach and based on the national resources approach which was implemented by the previous administration under the direction of the now right hon. Leader of the Opposition. What the Prime Minister has created in this regard and what he seems to intend to do is simply not enough.

Unless permanent consultative machinery is immediately improved, let me cite just two examples of things that could happen. The President of the Privy Council, to whom the Prime Minister intends to delegate the work of planning priorities, will virtually be unable to do his job without close liaison with the provinces. Another result would be the central government's inability to exercise proper control and direction over monetary policy. For example, what is going to happen when the province of Quebec has such great control over a funded pension plan? Consultation must be a permanent thing; the machinery for consultation must be permanent. Consultation with the provinces must be improved immediately. I know that I seem repetitive on this subject, Mr. Chairman, and my friends have often asked when I am going to stop whipping a dead horse; but I am going to speak and speak on this subject until the administration opposite takes at least partial cognizance of my suggestions.
At this point I should like to conclude my remarks by making some specific suggestions and proposals. Before further tax agreements can really be concluded with the provinces the constitution must be modernized; we must have a fresh look at sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act and the question of overlapping jurisdictions. We in the opposition are calling for a conference of federal-provincial leaders. Let us put first things first. Before satisfactory agreement on tax matters can be reached, let the federal and provincial leaders meet in order to redefine federal and provincial constitutional powers and, amongst other things, as the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said, seek proper constitutional amendment procedures here in Canada. Let it not be a meeting just for a few days. Much preparation-and other hon. members have made reference to this fact-will be necessary. The meeting itself might take many days; but I for one feel sure that the results will be more than worth while.
We might find that apart from the equalization formula and related principles many will agree that generally speaking the government that spends the tax dollar should raise it. If a provincial government, for example, does not participate in a federally sponsored plan, is it not preferable for the provincial government in question to recapture compensatory taxation powers rather than receive an annual, lump sum payment from the federal treasury? I just throw this out as a suggestion, Mr. Chairman.

Certainly the federal government has its responsibilities for maintaining and encouraging minimum standards in the economic and social fields. In Quebec, for example, wage levels and farmers' incomes are far below national standards. Poverty in our cities in Quebec is far greater than the national average. These conditions must be remedied by strong provincial and federal governments acting within their constitutional responsibilities. But this must be done consequent upon the conference to which I have referred being called immediately. While the Ottawa and the Quebec governments wrangle, the economic position of our poor in the cities and in the countryside, of our farmers and workers in the province of Quebec, does not improve one little bit. Much of the contemporary problem-I will not say all of it-in my province today is of an economic nature.
The vast majority of the people in my province know that we shall work out these problems within the framework of our confederation. Terrorists and ultra-separatists spurred on by alien forces have already taken a toll. I do not say this in a sensationalist way, but one might truly believe that the classical Leninist doctrine approach has been employed to create national disunity. I say these things not in the spirit of Mc-Carthyism.
Once there is agreement, after such a meeting, on the constitution as suggested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, and the meeting redefines the powers of and modernizes the constitution, federal-provincial tax problems and financial arrangements will be more easily arrived at. Then, and only then, an active central government will be able to take a strong federal position within the constitution. There will be no separation; there will be no opting out of confederation, just as a century ago there was no opting out of the United States union. But let us profit from many of the unhappy aspects of their experience. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, future tax and financial arrangements should only be concluded after such a federal-provincial constitutional conference is called. And it must be called immediately because from what the Minister of Finance said a few minutes ago, I am very much afraid that the present government, in going into these taxation conferences in the near future, are once again about to put the cart before the horse, which is something they seem to have a knack of doing-a penchant for doing, if you will, in federal-provincial problems.
Federal-Provincial Relations
My second suggestion relates to the immediate necessity for improving permanent consultative machinery; a real secretariat for federal-provincial affairs, based on the modern resources approach and the ARDA approach commenced by the last administration which I supported in this house, must be established. This type of permanent secretariat for federal-provincial affairs should be established on the prime minister's and premier's level.
It is my hope that these observations and proposals will be of some use at a time when all Canadians of good will are searching for avenues of understanding and moderation. Unity in diversity should be the keynote of this approach, at a time when, as 1 said before, the voices of extremism from all sides have long since received far more than their share of attention. Hard work and the willingness to listen and understand will be required. Yet realistic optimism dictates that good sense will prevail. I for one know that 1967 will be a great and happy celebration for Canada and all Canadians.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to oppose the resolution as presented by the Minister of Finance. I rise for the purpose of making some observations in connection with it. We have been reminded by the minister in his opening remarks in presenting the resolution to us that we should not be misled by the simple form of the resolution into thinking that it is not complicated and is not complex.
So with that in mind I approach the general substance of the resolution itself, and I say immediately that my experience and sympathy throughout my political life has been almost entirely-at least up to 1960 entirely-from the viewpoint of the provinces rather than the central government.
We now find that this subject which is before us is of tremendous importance. Federal-provincial relations in a country such as ours are always important; today I think they are more than ordinarily important. This has been brought about for a variety of reasons. We have heard the reasons referred to this afternoon in a good many most eloquent speeches. I listened with great interest and some benefit to the speech of my hon. friend and near neighbour, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue. I also listened to the hon. member for Yukon advancing the general needs of and urge for consideration which he felt for that part of Canada which he represents. We have just listened to our great

Federal-Provincial Relations friend, the young member for Brome-Missis-quoi, who gave the house in my opinion a very fine illustration of his intense conviction for the need for co-operative action in order that this great and dear country of ours shall continue to grow, flourish and prosper as an entity.
Consequently I find myself unable to talk of co-operative federalism. To me it is quite a difficult phrase to define. I might go to the dictionary but I would still find it difficult to define. I think there exists the general opinion, both inside and outside the chamber, in the hearts and minds of most Canadians that this is our country. It is Canada, and it is a Canada which is a whole rather than a series of parts. It is with that in mind that I confess I find myself changing my viewpoint to a certain extent; not that I do not want or think it necessary to advocate any further the needs of my native province, because I do. I would be derelict in my duty if I did not speak on behalf of my province and on behalf of the Atlantic provinces generally, because that was my training and that is my urge. But I do think we cannot get away from the general idea that we as Canadians must recognize the fact that we must view our country as a whole; that in discussing federal-provincial relations we shall consider nothing which should be done so far as the provinces are concerned at the expense of a strong central government.
I want to refer in general terms to some of the events in which I have been interested and of which I certainly have some knowledge with regard to dominion-provincial relations. During the period 1944 to 1952, as a member of the opposition in a provincial house I listened many times to the premier of the province making reports to the legislature concerning his success in conducting negotiations on behalf of the province, as one of a group attending a dominion-provincial conference. I remember many times his saying that the announced proposition was as good a proposition as was possible to make in light of the responsibilities of the federal administration at the time. We criticized as much as we could and to the extent that our intelligence and general knowledge permitted us. But generally speaking I was impressed by those words-that the province got as good a deal as it felt was justified in the light of the responsibilities of Canada as a nation. That was the sort of thing I listened to during that period of time. Then after 1952 I had some connection with provincial conferences.

Then a day or two ago, last Thursday to be exact, I listened with great interest and admiration to the speech of my leader, the Leader of the Opposition. I thought it was one of the finest speeches which had ever been delivered in this house. Not only was it fine from the point of view of advancing his arguments with the maximum amount of impression and knowledge, but he also suggested the particular need of today for the government to take some leadership in sponsoring what might be considered a "fathers of continuing confederation conference", a sort of new fathers of confederation conference. I am sure that is what my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi had in mind a few moments ago-another fathers of confederation conference, but this time a fathers of continuing confederation conference.
In my opinion, it is just as important and so much easier to keep something going which is already going than it is to start something new. I was greatly impressed with the speech of my leader, and I feel that the government can well take his suggestions to heart, and I hope they will. I trust that from the seed which he planted, which seed has been watered by quite a few hon. members here this afternoon, will come something which will be of great benefit to our country as a continuing great nation.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and continue my remarks at eight.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was referring to the speech made by my right hon. leader and to the fact that

in it he had referred to a speech made by the premier of Newfoundland in June, 1955. He quoted some extracts from that speech, and it just so happens that I listened to Premier Smallwood when he was making it. Before we become second class citizens of Canada we will show the other maritime provinces how to get out of confederation.
This indicated that at that time the premier of Newfoundland felt very strongly about the deal the Atlantic provinces were getting from the government of the day. The Prime Minister was a member of that government and also the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am not so sure whether my hon. friend the Minister of Transport also was a member.

speechtext:
Whether he pleads guilty or not, the point is that the government of that day disregarded Premier Smallwood's words and paid no attention whatsoever to them.
I want to come to the question of the discriminatory features which existed prior to the advent of the Diefenbaker government in 1957, and I want to quote some of the words which I myself uttered at the conference of 1955, speaking on behalf of the province of New Brunswick. I said this:
Yet, Mr. Chairman, most of us will admit that certain deficiencies and weaknesses in this course of national development have become very evident. It is true that Canada as a whole gained in prosperity and social security and all provinces have made considerable progress since 1945; yet, at the same time, the discriminatory features of our federal system have not been overcome and, in some respects, have tended to grow greater over the years.
New Brunswick has derived considerable benefits from federal social security provisions and no doubt this is true in any province where the low income groups are relatively great in number and
Federal-Provincial Relations
the per capita income tends to be low. Yet, although supplementary family income from social welfare sources is welcome and useful in raising regional standards of living, the fact remains that such matters still depend and must always depend upon the regional economy in the final analysis. It will be the submission on behalf of our province that this matter can only be dealt with by a national policy specifically designed to improve regional income through helping to increase the productive capacity of areas which fall below certain indices to be determined.
At that conference the second argument that was advanced was that future tax rental agreements should include a factor that would take into consideration the taxable capacity among the various provinces, and now, some years later, I say to the Minister of Finance that taxable capacity and ability must be taken into account in all considerations with the provinces at all times.
In 1955 we of the Atlantic provinces asked the government for special adjustment grants to make up our lack of taxable capacity or, in very plain language, our lack of ability to pay. However, there was no response and no action from the Liberal government of that day. We were told it was impossible to differentiate as between one part of Canada and another, and there was no response to that request until the government led by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition came into office.
I shall tell you, Mr. Chairman, where you can find the record of what took place at that time. As set out on page 5294 of Hansard for July 9 last you will see that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants listed there as item No. 8, and you will see that from the year 1958-59 in which they were introduced they totalled $25 million for the succeeding four years, and at the beginning of 1962-63 they were raised to $35 million and have continued on that basis until the present time. I simply wish to point out that this government is taking the benefit of a good example set by the previous administration in recognizing what was done in dealing fairly with the Atlantic provinces.
I also want to call the attention of the committee to the table placed on the record by the Minister of Finance, as recorded at page 5184 of Hansard for July 7 last, and to his remarks with respect to it when he says it shows the difference between the November 1963 proposals and the proposals of April 1964. There he states that the government of which he is a distinguished member had a change of heart in the matter of a few months and decided to give our provinces

Federal-Provincial Relations more money, but he does not say why it refused to give the provinces more money in the first instance.
Since an increase is shown I, as a New Brunswicker, am pleased to see my province will benefit, but in the minister's speech he did not say where he proposed to get the funds that he is abating to the provinces. They amount to a considerable sum of money, an additional $87 million for the current year, an additional $171 million for next year, and an additional $246 million for 1966-67. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance has forgotten that expression, "a balanced budget" which he used many times in this chamber when he was over here in opposition. I wonder whether he would acknowledge that he favours deficit spending indefinitely and forevermore.
Does he favour deficit spending in a buoyant economy? It is my understanding of economics, to the extent that I may have some knowledge of that subject, that deficit spending is used when things are declining, when it is necessary to make provision for employment and when it is necessary to do something of an unusual nature to stimulate the economy. That is the time when, according to the economists, deficit spending is justified. We hear our friends opposite bragging day after day about the buoyant economy, while at the same time they do not say where the funds are going to come from to balance the budget. That expression has not been used by them since they were over here on this side of the house.
So as a Canadian I am wondering where the minister proposes to get the money which he is abating to the provinces. In my opinion there is only one place to get it and that is by additional taxation. I think he owes it to the house to say what he proposes to tax, on what items he is going to impose tax and on what items already taxed he is going to raise the tax. These are things which I think we in this house have a right to know and to which so far he has made absolutely no reference at all. It seems to me that he owes the house more explanation than he has given us up to now.
I find no fault with the extra money for the provinces. I find no fault with the expenditure of money itself. As a matter of fact, I am rather favourable to the spending of money by governments, but I do not think the spending of money by governments should go on at a time of a buoyant economy when presumably things are as good as they can be, and still make no attempt to balance the


budget, but pass the increasing debt along to our children and our children's children to pay some time in the future. In my opinion such a policy is completely unjustified at the present time and the house certainly should ask the Minister of Finance and the government to explain what they are going to do about it.
I think the minister should also have some understanding with the provinces, and perhaps through them with the municipalities as well, relative to financing. I have in mind that we as a parliament consider that the control of the monetary system, control of inflation and in general the credit of the country are and should be in the hands of the federal government. I do not think there is any question about that in the minds of any of us. But when the provinces and the municipalities are allowed to budget for deficits year after year, then year after year the money stream must of necessity be increased by that amount. It seems to me that unless there is an element of control in some way, either by agreement or otherwise, we cannot help but be bound to get a degree of inflation, with all the evils that go with it. So I think from the standpoint of the general good of Canada there must be an understanding with the provinces so that the whole question of credit, money supply and the monetary system in itself can be determined in the light of the economics of the whole country.
The Leader of the Opposition has suggested a conference on the whole question of federal-provincial relations. This afternoon the minister had some advice as to certain machinery that had been set up at the last conference with the provinces, but in my opinion that is purely on an administrative level. We have to have something more than just a set-up of people who are charged with duties and responsibilities of administration in order to deal with this most important matter of the relationship between the federal government and the provinces, both economic and political.
As I said before the supper recess, in my opinion it has become necessary to set up a second fathers of confederation conference so that there may be a genuine attempt made at the highest level possible to meet the political and economic difficulties which exist in this country, and deal with them with perhaps about the same state of mind that existed 100 years ago. We have no way of knowing that the difficulties of the fathers of confederation then were not greater even

than the difficulties facing us today. I do not think we have any particular reason to feel that the particular difficulties facing us today are insurmountable, not by any means; but I do think it is the duty of the government to furnish leadership to the country at the present time in this matter. They should set up a conference of this nature, and the mechanics thereof are a matter which they in their judgment might determine. I think something certainly should be done and in my view the suggestion put forward by my leader is one which deserves the greatest amount of consideration.
Such a conference should be a meeting of the representatives of the federal and provincial governments. It might take the form of a centennial celebration to a certain extent. We are getting close to the 100 years. I would hope that such a group would be just as dedicated as the fathers of confederation were 100 years ago and just as determined to succeed as they were then. I think they would be no less determined to keep Canada together than their predecessors were to establish this great nation.
There should be some knowledge available to the federal government relative to the budget position of all the provinces. As has been pointed out many times in this chamber by the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi, there should be the closest kind of cooperation. I see by the clock, Mr. Chairman, that my time has expired. I am pleased to have the opportunity of expressing the opinions I have voiced in the last 20 minutes and in the 10 minutes immediately before the supper recess. I trust the minister will take due note of all these words of wisdom which have fallen from my lips and I thank the house for listening.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, a former premier, may create some difficulty for me. It was on July 9 that the motion really came up for debate following the statement the evening before by the minister. The resolution we are discussing this evening is in these words:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the revision of certain fiscal arrangements with the provinces and to provide adjustments of fiscal arrangements and taxation provisions consequential upon the provision of youth allowances to parents resident in certain provinces.
In dealing with the sharing of taxation between the federal government and the provinces, some of us who are not quite so eloquent as some of the orators we heard this
Federal-Provincial Relations afternoon may want to come to grips with the economics of the situation. I think that all members of parliament, no matter what government is in office, feel somewhat sympathetic toward the minister of finance. He is the minister in the cabinet who has to find the money for all expenditures. He is the minister who has to pay the bill resulting from any arrangements made between the federal government and the provinces.
All of us appreciate one fact, that every government at whatever level, the local level, provincial level or federal level, is struggling to meet the bills for certain programs today. We have heard a lot about the province of Quebec today, but whether it is western Canada, Ontario or the maritimes the local governments are involved in a great struggle to try to find the finances necessary to enable them to carry out the jobs they are supposed to perform.
The provincial governments are practically in the same boat. Some governments claim they have done a better job of financing than others. I saw my good freind, the hon. member for Red Deer, just recently talking to the Minister of Finance. He may have been discussing debt free money with the Minister of Finance. In the last few years I know the Minister of Finance would have been most interested in debt free money-at least, free of debt. The hon. member for Ontario suggests that the present minister voted for it. I can appreciate that.
Then, one comes to the point of local government. In any city, whether it is my home city of Calgary or any other city in Canada, property taxes have now reached such a height that the advantages that governments provided during the last ten years, whether they be Conservative governments or Liberal governments, through the National Housing Act in assisting the average worker to get a home, have been lost. The property taxes at the local level are so high that many workers are unable to live in these houses that we, in parliament, have tried to provide.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: And wait until next spring.

speechtext:
They will probably be higher. The provincial governments say they cannot give any more help to the municipalities because they are having trouble balancing their budgets. If you are great jugglers, such as the premier of British Columbia or the people in the debt free province of Alberta, you do not run into these problems because

Federal-Provincial Relations you have good bookkeepers. My good friends on my left clap. The fact is if you add up the municipal debt in Alberta and the provincial debt of Alberta you will find that on a per capita basis it is as high as that of the province of Manitoba or the province of Saskatchewan, if not higher.
I have never been too friendly with the socialist government. I have said some very unkind things about them. However they balanced their budget and they left their house in very good order when they turned it over to Mr. Thatcher.
The point I want to make is that all levels of government are struggling. We pass legislation to help people obtain houses, give them new houses or let them live in better apartment blocks. But property taxes are so high, provincial tax levels are so high-and so are federal levels-that we are all feeling the squeeze. The problem finally falls on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance. If he does not perform some miracle, everything goes wrong. I am not going to enter into a debate on the criticisms of a former minister of finance, Mr. Donald Fleming. There was a lot of abuse heaped on him. There has been a lot of abuse heaped on this Minister of Finance. When he goes, there will be a lot of abuse heaped on the next minister of finance. I am sure the former minister of finance, who is sitting here to my left, will corroborate the fact that you have got to find the money somewhere, and you cannot perform a miracle.
I am sure that if I were a mouse and wandered into a meeting of the Liberal cabinet or the Conservative cabinet, I would hear the minister of finance saying, "Just a minute; stop; where is the money coming from?"

speechtext: Are you the mouse that roared?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I would not know about that, but I would say that I would put up a good roar if I were a mouse.
Then we come to the second problem. These are problems we have to face at the economic level. We are talking about equalization payments across the board for all provinces. If we were to return to the old scheme whereby each province collected its own taxes, that is income taxes and succession duties, we would find this worked a hardship on some provinces, not because wealth was not produced in those provinces but because after the people built up wealth in a province


they retired to some other province. For instance, in so far as the prairie provinces are concerned, people retire to British Columbia where the climate is a little better for them to spend their declining days.
When you look at succession duties you find that the duty on stocks and bonds is paid at the point where the company has its headquarters. As a result provinces like Saskatchewan, and even Alberta have suffered from this regulation. This was true, even before Alberta had this windfall-and whether that was the result of the government or oil, I have never been able to determine. My friends seem to indicate they think it resulted from oil. I still want to be fair and I say this provincial government in Alberta has done a pretty good job. Perhaps I am a little prejudiced.
The point I want to make is that this tax revenue falls to the province in which these stock certificates have their headquarters. Now we have got into a new kind of taxation, and some people call this centralization. I am not going to agree with one speaker from this side this afternoon who indicated we do not need a strong central government, because I think we do. I am going to have something more to say about that. The point is that in attempting to arrive at a system of taxation that would be equitable and fair for all Canadians we said, "All right, the federal government is going to collect these taxes. Then we will try to distribute them provincially throughout the land on an equitable basis." I am referring to succession duties and income taxes. This resulted from the fact that people would sell their capital or other assets at a certain price and retire to another province which would benefit from the succession duties.
First of all, over the land you had an equalization of the system of taxation. This was necessary. I think I can quote a very distinguished premier in a few minutes on this point. Everyone in the house, irrespective of where he sits, will admit that a Conservative government did a very fair job of setting up a new equalization system so far as the provinces are concerned. I have been sometimes critical of Premier Lesage. Sometimes you have to see what other people are saying and thinking. Sometimes the people are called fanatics and whom I call the insane people, sitting on the fringe, seem to get more publicity because the people who think logically forget to get their ideas across to the people in this land. Mr. Lesage

paid quite a compliment to the former Conservative government, as will be seen when one reads page 28 of the brief he presented November 25, 1963. Perhaps I had better name this report. It is a statement by Hon. Jean Lesage, premier, minister of finance and of federal-provincial affairs, delivered to the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa, November 25, 1963. It is interesting to note that he admitted what had been done. This is what he said:
From several vantage points, the results of the 1960-61 federal-provincial conference-
I pause there to say that certainly was a conference under a Conservative government.
-showed progress as compared with the former situation.
Mr. Lesage said this when he met with the new government.
We do not underestimate this progress.
In other words, he did not underestimate the progress made during a Conservative regime so far as establishing an equitable basis for sharing taxes was concerned. I hear one of my friends laugh. Well I guess he laughed at Mr. Lesage because he laughs at other Liberals. These are Mr. Lesage's words, not mine. I quote again from Mr. Lesage:
On other points however we have several reservations which show why we are bringing these matters up again today.
I might say when you read the whole brief presented by Mr. Lesage you will find he says in effect "We have made these points before; we are not adding anything new on the record, but we have made progress under a Conservative government and we hope we are going to make as much progress under the new Liberal government." This is the compliment that was paid by the premier of Quebec. So there was a beginning so far as this matter is concerned, a very sound beginning.
We come back to this situation. The Conservative government did work in conjunction with some of the premiers to bring about more equitable taxation between the local level, the provincial level and the federal level. The provincial premiers admit this, and this was a sound beginning. I am going to say this: I should like to conduct a Gallup poll in the province of Quebec. We hear a lot from a certain premier, and I do not know whether or not there are fringe benefits, but there are fringes, anyhow, on the question.
I question whether the people of the province of Quebec think exactly the way these people who pump out their propaganda would 20220-343
Federal-Provincial Relations seem to indicate. I think they are as good Canadians as the people of Ontario and western Canada. I believe they think of Canada first. I have never found fault with any premier who comes down to meet the prime minister of Canada, whether the prime minister was Conservative or Liberal, and stands up for his province.
Look at what Alberta has to say. I have paid a compliment to the premier of Alberta and I will pay him another. He presented his brief, and he said exactly the same as Premier Lesage-that a sound beginning had been made under the Conservative government and that it was naturally hoped that this good work would be carried on by the new administration. It is a strange thing that every time the Liberals come in there is some sensitivity in reference to confederation. I do not believe that sensitivity exists to such a degree as is made out. I think it comes from those who want to pump out propaganda and generate-"generate"; that's a good word; it is better than the one I would have used-a whole lot of trouble. If Premier Lesage says he is satisfied to the extent that he has made progress, I think he is satisfied, because I do not think there is anyone in Canada who will say that Premier Lesage is not an aggressive premier who speaks up for his province.
What does the premier of Alberta have to say? The Alberta brief is not as weighty. There is not so much raw material, perhaps. The Alberta program probably did not rate so big a brief. The former minister of finance said we had more oil and therefore did not need as much money. But I do not think Premier Manning would go along with that, because we are always looking for new revenue. What did he say? He said that among the specific matters to which the conference should give attention, the government of Alberta regarded the following as being of particular importance. Then three points are mentioned, and I would say this: These three points are practically identical with the requests contained in Mr. Lesage's brief. This is what he said:
The necessity to evolve an arrangement under which each government will be assured sufficient financial resources to enable it to discharge its constitutional responsibilities without loss of its rightful sovereignty and without imposing oppressive burdens of taxation and debt upon its people.
Premier Manning said that. If Premier Lesage had said that, some of the French people would say: He wants to break away from confederation. I am sure Premier Maiming

Federal-Provincial Relations does not want to break away from confederation. But I would say this: If we allow these fanatical people-fanatics I say, almost insane in their propaganda-to get away with it in Canada, then the rest of Canada is going to fall to the United States; and I believe there is not one thinking person in Quebec, from the premier downward, who does not believe that whatever the situation has been culturally, economically or constitutionally, the people have had a better deal under confederation in a country called Canada than they would get if this country was taken over by the United States-with the greatest respect to the United States, because I am Canadian first.
It is time we understood what is going on. The premiers of the west are not really saying much that is different from Premier Lesage. It is the interpretations which differ, particularly when they are irresponsible. On page 2 of the brief, Premier Manning said:
The provision of effective incentives to stimulate more active economic growth and the forms such incentives should take and the means by which they can best be provided.
He, too, criticized in some degree-and I am not quarrelling with him-these shared programs, because they push a province into a position where it has to dip into its resources in order to find money to help carry out these projects. On page 40 of his brief Premier Lesage says exactly the same thing.
So these two provincial premiers are not very far apart, and if that is so it seems to me we are not in very much trouble as far as confederation is concerned, because all of us press for benefits for the part of the country we live in, wherever it may be-in Alberta, if we live in Alberta, or Saskatchewan if we live in Saskatchewan, or Quebec if we live in Quebec. That is Canadian; there is nothing wrong with it.
Further on he says this:
Other joint programs have barely been started. This is more particularly the case in Quebec since 1960. Financial equivalence should therefore take into account the cost of these plans, had they been allowed to reach what might be called their "maturity". Briefly, if Quebec does not count on the abolition of conditional grants and on the financial equivalence which would result therefrom to obtain otherwise not expected revenues, there will be no question either of Quebec being satisfied with anything other than its fair share of federal funds.
Premier Manning has said practically the same thing. When the leader of the New Democratic party was premier of Saskatchewan I heard him present his brief on one occasion and, as is proper, he fought for his

province. He should have fought for it; he was the premier of that province. But there is a disturbing factor. It might have been carelessness or it might have been overenthusiasm in the heat of an election campaign, but the Liberal party went out and promised certain programs without consulting the provinces. They said: We will bring them in within 60 days. This was so they could look like great men. Then they brought in this legislation later on in the absence of consultation and, as a result, we did get some sensitivity about confederation. And if Mr. Lesage stood up and said "Just a minute" to the Prime Minister of Canada, he was right. And if Mr. Manning stood up and said "Just a minute" to the Prime Minister of Canada, he was right, too; because we in the Conservative party believe that one must consult the provinces in this regard. Why? Because under confederation, according to the sections of the law which divide jurisdiction between the provinces and the federal government, certain powers go to the provinces and certain powers are retained by the federal government. That is the position according to the constitution. Therefore the Prime Minister and his government should have consulted with the premier of Quebec and with the premiers of the other provinces before they tried to thrust certain programs down people's throats. That is what happened. And when hon. gentlemen over there learn to be less arrogant, to be less overbearing and to have a greater sense of humility, there will be a strengthening of the fabric of confederation because then you will not have the sensitivity which now exists, although it has been blown up out of all proportion.
I move around this land. I talk to French Canadians and to people out in British Columbia. Essentially, every Canadian thinks the same. He wants to keep Canada Canadian and make sure that every Canadian lives with dignity with his family. Every government, irrespective of criticism which has been directed toward it, has tried to implement such a program, with the one exception of the new government which came in last April. The government which was led by Mr. St. Laurent did consult the provinces. But hon. gentlemen opposite failed to do so and this was because they were pledged to take some kind of action within 60 days.
So there is the situation. If there is any trouble with regard to confederation, responsibility lies on the shoulders of those who sit on the treasury benches-and those benches

are vacant, so it does not weigh too heavily. We westerners are not very good diplomats. I think the Minister of Finance will agree with that. But if confederation is to proceed untroubled, there must be tolerance and there must be compromise. I do not mean the kind of wishy-washy compromise which would divide this country. It must be tolerance and compromise based on national responsibility. Any other kind becomes appeasement, and appeasement will destroy, never create. If we read through the pages of history, whether of national or international affairs, we find that wishy-washy appeasement always brings about disunity.
So I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that one thing we should certainly have is tolerance of one another. Certainly we must make compromises at all levels of government, but there must be the kind of tolerance and compromise that is responsible or this country will be destroyed. We have a lot of wishy-washy nonsense talked about expenditures, and how we are going to go it alone. No section of this country can go it alone, because if you look at the budget of this country you will appreciate that we spend $7 billion a year, and the greatest proportion of that expenditure is for defence. We know that today we get into local and parochial arguments and disputes and talk about dividing some parts of this country from the rest.
I tell you, Mr. Chairman, that we face a new situation in this world. We must keep our partnerships in the western world, whether we have the threat of the cold war or not, because there is a new kind of communism that even the old kind of communist fears; and we need all the strength we have in the western world, whether it is the strength of 19 million people in Canada or the strength of all the peoples in NATO and the defence of this continent in NORAD. When we talk about dividing this country we should start thinking about our grandchildren, because our grandchildren's chance of survival in the kind of life our forefathers came here to build will only remain and be perpetuated if we stay together as a nation and internationally.
This political nonsense-I do not want to single anyone out and I would not single out any one party; but I could single out a few individuals-that is spread in this country, the talk about Quebec leaving confederation or any other province leaving confederation, does nothing to help unity; because if they left it would only be on borrowed time and before long there would be some new threat

Compare this with any other parliament and you will realize we are doing a little better than we did in previous parliaments. This is most important. We have done very well this session. But whatever the reason, we have done a little better and the word is proceeding. Thirty eight items have been passed, and this is a little better than average. As far as I am concerned, as one who observes parliament from day to day, this parliament is going along normally. You may ask me a question when I am through speaking. He does not really like to hear these comments, Mr. Chairman, but this is the basis upon which Alberta has developed its resources and municipal finance, so that today there are more towns and villages complete with sewage systems and water development, and more miles of paved roads simply because they have used their own resource capital for the development of their municipal and city areas. But this is not the question to argue about tonight, because even provinces such as Alberta or British Columbia, which have been able to balance their books and run things in rather an efficient way down through the last number of years, today face problems which even their administrations are going to find very difficult to overcome.
The reason is simply this. Under the policies of the federal government we are faced at the present time with a situation where the sum total of government expenditure, provincial and federal, tends to be much more than the sum total of government income. Last year-as I mentioned the other night- the federal and provincial governments of Canada spent well over $1 billion more than they took in. The situation is going to be worse this year, simply because under the limitations of the present system there is no other alternative; and unless something is done to change this situation we are really going to be in financial difficulties. It all comes back to the question of the provincial fiscal arrangements that are in existence at the present time. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that it does not really matter so much how these provincial fiscal arrangements are juggled; it is the taxpayer who

pays the tax dollar and it is he who is carrying this ever spiralling burden of tax load that is heaped upon his back.
Therefore I would suggest to the committee that unless we face up to this issue and get at the fundamental cause of the situation, merely doctoring it up as we are doing is not going to change anything or help the situation at all. After all, it is the taxpayer who pays the tax dollar. While we may talk in this house a great deal about how we are going to adjust the expenditure of the money that is collected from taxes or borrowed in the taxpayers' name, how we are going to change our basis of sharing this tax income does not matter because under our present system with regard to debt, it is bound to increase and the tax load will go up with it.
As I mentioned the other night, 15 per cent of all our federal income goes just in paying the service cost of our federal debt. Likewise there are similar difficulties in most of the provinces. Even more difficult than provincial or federal financing is the question of municipal financing. There are literally scores of municipal governments in this country today which have borrowed up to the hilt and cannot borrow any more. This is because the debt burden they carry is more than their normal tax load can manage. So I am absolutely convinced it is essential that in dealing with this subject we must face this thing at its very roots.
One of the ways in which our provincial and municipal governments could be helped so much more than they can be helped by juggling our provincial fiscal arrangements is to make available that capital which is necessary for capital development, and to make it available on an entirely different basis than what we are doing at the present time. We have talked a good deal about social capital, the term accepted today across the country to describe the money necessary for the development of our social capital needs. Rather than operate on a deficit basis as we are at the present time there is no reason at all why such social capital cannot be made available through the Bank of Canada, under a separate arm of the Bank of Canada such as is the industrial development bank. On such a basis we could really provide the assistance to the provinces which the provinces need so urgently, and will be able to help them a little out of the crisis they face because of the problems which are part of the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements about which we are talking tonight.

The other day in speaking to this resolution I referred to the remarks the minister had made when he presented the resolution to the house. The minister expressed concern about the continuing increase in deficits, and said there is a limit beyond which the federal government cannot go. To me this brought to mind a statement made previous to these remarks, in which he said that during this coming fiscal year he expected there would be a deficit of $455 million according to the traditional method of accounting. At that time I asked him a series of questions, and I referred to his reference to traditional methods of accounting. If we could have the answers to the questions which I posed to him, I believe we would have answers which would show that it is possible to provide social capital needed in this country without the tremendous debt load it carries today. I want to put these questions back on the record, and I do so because this afternoon-

Federal-Provincial Relations fund as the result of the interest paid on these bonds. My point is that if this can be done as far as our present financing is concerned, why cannot it be done to assist the provinces and the municipalities as well?
Another question I asked the other night was: What portion of these charges, this accrual of interest charges on government bonds, is returned to the consolidated revenue fund? I believe the minister owes it to the committee to answer these questions, because in the answers to these questions he the solutions to some of the problems the provinces are facing. Mr. Chairman, I only want to take a few minutes of the time of the committee to comment on the minister's opening statement about the tremendous degree of amity which has been Canada's experience over the last year, ever since the Liberals came to power, in terms of federal-provincial relations. I cannot let his statement that there has been nothing but love go by unchallenged. Tonight I want to discuss this subject for a few minutes because in fact there has been absolutely no consultation, ever since the Liberal government came to power, between the federal government and the governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend and colleague from the Yukon covered most of this in his remarks earlier today and I will not repeat what he said. Surely it will suffice to point out to the committee that I think there has been little respect shown for consultation and little indication of concern on the part of the minister or his colleagues for the people in the north. In fact, the Liberal government have been so concerned that they have allowed the government of the Northwest Territories to lapse and go out of being completely, so that for a period of four and a half months last winter, from December to March at any rate, we never had even a legislative council in the Northwest Territories. That is the extent to which this government is concerned about democracy in some 50 per cent of Canada.
Perhaps I may be permitted to point to another example. Ever since the twenty sixth parliament the hon. member for Yukon speaking for the Yukon, and I representing the Northwest Territories, have been asking the federal government to allow the governments

Federal-Provincial Relations Of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to sit in on federal-provincial conferences. It may come as a surprise to the members of this committee, indeed to the public at large, to learn that the territorial governments of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are not allowed to sit in on these federal-provincial conferences, not even as observers. When I look up the index for the first session of the twenty sixth parliament I find that on five different occasions I pleaded with the federal government to allow us representation at these conferences, and every time I was turned down. I find that the hon. member for Yukon made the same request six times. On looking at what has gone on since the second session commenced I find that the hon. member for Yukon and I have each on six different occasions begged this government to allow the Yukon and Northwest Territories to send an observer to these meetings, to this tremendous consultation which is going on, and we were refused every time.
Twenty four times in the last 15 months we have asked the government, "Would you give those of us who live in the north a chance to have a representative sit in at your meetings?", and the answer we have received is that we are to be represented at the federal-provincial conferences by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who is going to negotiate for us in a hard-headed bargaining type of way. What kind of nonsense is this? To what extent is the minister going to get up on his hind legs and defend the interests of the north?
When the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of Justice got up and said to the minister of northern affairs, "We are going to sell the Eskimos, in order to make a little deal over here with the province of Quebec" to what extent did the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources stand up and say, "You shall not make a deal to sell these people." If it had not been for the official opposition the deal would have been made.

Mr. Chairman, if I am allowed to have the floor now, I will continue. When the Minister of Finance said that everything was tremendously smooth I was interested in what he said as recorded at page 5,181 of Hansard for July 7 last:

I had to have some sort of introduction.
That is how he explained what he had been saying. So far as the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are concerned there has been no consultation since the government took office. The minister's statement is completely misleading in its application to what the truth is in the north, and I have no reason to accuse the minister of telling the truth in southern Canada either. As a northerner it seems to me that we are not to be allowed consultation in federal-provincial matters.
Do the federal ministers really understand the needs of the country? If we are not allowed to have our own people at these conferences we want to know to what extent the ministry knows about northern matters. I shall give two examples, and one is the fascinating statement made by the Minister of Agriculture as recorded at page 5239 of Hansard for July 9, when he was asked to what extent the government was going to implement its program of free milk for children in Canadian schools. The minister was fresh from a breakfast he had just thrown for some 3,000 people in Calgary where they cooked up 350 dozen eggs and this minister, with his hands spread across the fullness of his being, said that most Canadian children are so full of milk that they cannot possibly hold any more.
Let me read to the minister and his colleagues a little bit of what in fact is the truth of the situation among some thousands of children in the Canadian north, and I may say this is not just in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I am quoting from page 224 of the Hall commission report-and I suggest to the fulsome Minister of Agriculture that he should read it before making these kinds of statements.
"Inhuman"-is the way a public health nurse described, in the course of a conversation, the living conditions of the Eskimos in her community. An apt description indeed. To realize this one has to shed the romantic ideas of Eskimo life, derived from children's books and movies, and walk through a settlement of Eskimo tents on a cold September night with the wind and rain lashing against the flimsy tents, babies crying and whimpering, and children and adults alike coughing inside. Outside is the stench of human and dog excretion and of rotten food scraps. The tent houses not only the family but all their belongings and implements-
Substantial beginnings have been made against the odds of northern logistics in the provision of health services, housing and some means of sanitation. Nevertheless, hundreds of families still live under conditions that would not be tolerated elsewhere even in a more moderate climate.

The members of the commission were so staggered by conditions that they made a recommendation saying:
While it is beyond our terms of reference to make recommendations in these related fields, we suggest that considerations of humanity and economics make it imperative for governments to to take comprehensive and practical actions in these related fields because without them the serious health problems facing Canadians everywhere but particularly in the north cannot be adequately and effectively resolved.
I am using this merely as an example, but I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he go back into the next meeting of this multimillionaire cabinet that characterizes the government and tell his colleagues what is going on and ask them to reinstate this program for free milk for school children in the Canadian north, many of whom do without milk from the time they are weaned. If he has any doubt about what I say is true I defy him to go to the Minister of Transport and ask him if it is true that the children in Newfoundland are so stuffed with milk that they cannot possibly stand any more nutrition.
I shall give another example of the kind of thought and ignorance that characterizes the government in terms of northern needs. Today I asked the Acting Prime Minister if the government would consider giving everyone in the Northwest Territories the right to vote. I asked this because the Prime Minister is over in London telling the people of the world that the commonwealth must give leadership in seeing to it that people of all colours, creeds and levels have an equal chance of citizenship. The Acting Prime Minister got up and said he did not understand; that there was no logical connection between these two statements.
Surely the government is aware that there are 10,000 Canadian citizens in the north, mostly Eskimos, who are not allowed to vote for their councillors who make their laws on education, on health, on furs, trapping and liquor. Surely he must have answered facetiously. I have a couple of quotations here that I simply will not deny to the committee, relating to the visit of the Prime Minister of Frobisher Bay. He was on his way from the breakfast party for the 3,000 people in Calgary, this great breakfast orgy the Minister of Agriculture had. It was not like the Roman orgies; it could only be compared to the orgies the barbarians had after they sacked Rome. This is a press report from the Edmonton Journal of July 7 last:

The Pearsons were surrounded by flag-waving children who giggled delightedly whenever Mr. Pearson gave them a friendly pat on the head. Eskimo women, with babies packed on their backs, puffed on cigarettes, smiling proudly with each prime ministerial greeting.
"I am very happy to be with you tonight," Mr. Pearson said. "We are all Canadians-the only difference is that you were here before we were."
If the Prime Minister wanted to tell the truth to those Eskimo people he could have told them about a few other differences. For example, he could have told them, "You are not allowed to vote for your own territorial legislators who make your laws on fur, game, liquor and education.'' He did not say to the Eskimos, "Your men have a life expectancy of 26 years and your women of 21J years, while ours in the south is 60 years." He did not say to them, "Your infant mortality rate, my fine Eskimo friends, is four times as high as that in the south, and 40 per cent of your grandchildren will never live to celebrate their first birthday." He did not tell them, "Death from infectious diseases among you is ten times as high as among us in the south and you will have ten times more deaths from tuberculosis." He did not tell them, "Ninety per cent of your men are unemployed,"-at a time when the Minister of Labour is saying that unemployment is now a seasonal thing in Canada. He did not say to them, although it amazed me, that they are so stuffed with milk they need nothing from now on but three maple leaves to be happy.
A new book has just come out, and before the Prime Minister or any of his multimillionaire cabinet visit Frobisher Bay again I suggest they read it. It is a book entitled "Eskimo Administration, Canada", and it is written by Dr. Diamond Jenness, a world renowned authority. It has just been published, and because the statistics I have already given on infant mortality are taken from this book I will do nothing more than read parts of the index: chapter 1, "Government Myopia", chapter 2, "Wards of the Police", chapter 3, "A Shackled Administration", chapter 4, "A Shackled Administration (continued)", chapter 5, "Bureaucracy in Inaction", chapter 10, "Steering Without a Compass". And so on. It is sickening. Yet the Minister of Agriculture, fresh from a breakfast of 350 dozen scrambled eggs, says that Canadian children are so full of milk we cannot get any more into them. Shame.

Here we go, Mr. Chairman, with that great Grit argument that says that since things were not done before, they need do nothing more. I have said in the house before that the great belief of Liberalism is that you do nothing except take office and that by some strange osmosis, by some mysterious alchemy, everybody in Canada is better off. The Minister of Agriculture stands there and says: Why, we are drinking sillabub in Calgary, and everywhere else everybody is full of milk. I do not know what the minister is full of, but Canadians in my part of the country are not full of milk.
With respect to the whole matter of federal-provincial relations it is frightening to me when I see nothing being done in the Canadian north. In the last 15 months federal spending has in fact dried up. When I think of the projects which are now in the process of offering hope to the people, I realize that not a single one of them has been started in the last 15 months. They are all merely carryovers. I do not mean they are not good. The Great Slave lake railway will penetrate the Northwest Territories. For the first time on August 10 steel will have crossed the 60th parallel. Every Liberal in the House of Commons voted against the Great Slave lake railway when the bill was before the house. Telecommunications are in fact being extended down to the Arctic ocean, but this is not a new program; it was started three years ago. The same is true of school construction.
What is frightening to me as a northener is that the tremendous effort put forward in the five years of Conservative administration was merely a beginning. When the hon.


member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon-La-prairie asks whether these terrible conditions among the Eskimos existed in 1962, the truthful answer is yes, they did. Certainly they did. But the fact of the matter is that in 1962 some 60 per cent of the Eskimo children at least had access to schools compared with less than 15 per cent in 1957.
I am one who has never tried to suggest in the house since being elected that all the answers were provided by the Conservatives, but the groundwork of schools, nursing stations, hospitals, communications, airports and roads was laid. A good start had been made, against tremendous opposition by the members of the opposition of that day, the Liberal party of Canada. They said it was a nightmare. I am not going to repeat all the things they said. Let it be clearly understood that the facilities that were then being provided were nothing more than the groundwork. At no time did the previous administration ever say that everything was solved and that there was nothing but harmony, sweetness and light in the Canadian north.
The previous administration said many times-I used this at the time I was campaigning; it was true then and is still true- that the maddeningly slow job of counteracting the terrible human problems had begun. What frightens me and what I lay at the doorstep of the present administration is that they have cancelled this program, and I suggest that the things they have done are not worthy of respect.
One or two programs that perhaps did have a bit of imagination when applied in the south are completely stupid when viewed in a northern context. I think of the winter house construction program. I would love to read the Minister of Labour some of the letters I have received from northerners who are trying to qualify for the $500 bonus under a program that contained no special provision for transportation problems long after the rivers are frozen up and you cannot ship stuff in there. The program made no provision for climatic conditions. One of my constituents said to me: I am sure the Minister of Labour does not know whether he is talking about Hay River in the Northwest Territories or Florida.
I think of how the Minister of Labour said in the house that the government was going to lessen the number of months in which municipalities can qualify for the municipal winter works program. He said that winter in this country only extended

from late November to early March. I do not know when winter ends in Inverness-Rich-mond or wherever he comes from but I can tell the house that I was at Cambridge Bay and Coppermine in the Northwest Territories about 10 days ago and the water is still frozen, with the result that the ships will not get in for a while yet.
Ever since the government took office there has been a complete absence of any reference to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Just a few weeks ago the hon. member for Yukon proposed a resolution that would have done something in terms of tax relief for the north. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, who is a bit of a northern expert by virtue of having made two trips in a DC-3, talked out the resolution. He said: No, this is not a good thing for northerners; if there is anything that would harm them it would be an income tax reduction. His remarks were fascinating and not only in terms of their strange logic because it is usually that embryo leader of the Liberal party in Ontario, the hon. member for Renfrew South, who does these things. But here we had the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources saying: No, no, from my vast and profound experience of the Canadian north the people do not need a tax reduction. It is a bit like the Minister of Agriculture saying that children do not need milk.

speechtext: How many trips did he make?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
He made two trips. Having made these remarks I am going to close with a plea to the government. I want them to be a bit like the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he said: Well, if I said that I was obviously wrong. I want them to admit their mistakes. I want them to resolve that in the interests of the poor, ragged and tattered people who frequent Canada's north they will depart from this policy of helping only those areas where the most federal seats are.
The charge has been made that the Liberal party has never really cared about equal opportunities for Canadians, that they only worry about those places where they can get the most federal seats. There are people who believe this is one reason why the change was so obvious under the previous administration, in that for the first time in Canada the maritimes, the west and the north received a fair share of the federal treasury.
